title: Curios of the Week #172
author: Ashman, Greg
summary: Greg Ashman's Curios of the Week #172 is a weekly education roundup curated from Ashman's vantage point as an Australian secondary science teacher and evidence-based education advocate. This installment covers the release of a Green Paper by the Teachers' Professional Association of Australia (TPAA), a research item on devices in schools, and additional sections (umbrella review, wellbeing intervention, gender-neutral pronouns) that were behind the subscriber paywall. The TPAA Green Paper argues that Australian schools suffer from excessive bureaucratization -- with bureaucrat-to-teacher ratios of 1:2 in Victoria and Queensland -- and that eliminating non-productive administrative posts would enable meaningful teacher pay increases. Ashman endorses the paper's critique of critical pedagogy but notes the problem is broader: schools are bombarded by bad ideas from everywhere, not only critical pedagogy. The roundup reflects Ashman's characteristic editorial stance: evidence-focused, skeptical of progressive pedagogical trends, and attentive to systemic and structural factors that constrain effective teaching. Note: The full issue was subscriber-paywalled; this summary covers the portions available in the subscriber email.
points: * TPAA's Green Paper documents a bureaucratic ratio of 1 administrator for every 2 teachers in Victoria and Queensland, with none of the initiatives these roles justify demonstrating positive outcomes -- arguing that restructuring would fund significant teacher pay increases. * The TPAA and its Green Paper represent the growing Red Union alternative to traditional teacher unions in Australia, explicitly offering representation to teachers who do not want to indirectly fund a political party through union dues. * Academic critics labeled TPAA an astroturf organization in a 2024 paper -- but Ashman notes the researchers disclosed they were supporters of traditional unions, one of which funded the research, undermining the paper's credibility. * Ashman endorses the Green Paper's critique of critical pedagogy but widens the diagnosis: the problem is not limited to one ideology but reflects a systemic failure of reality checks and accountability that allows bad ideas of all kinds to persist. * The roundup reflects Ashman's characteristic editorial stance: evidence-focused, skeptical of progressive pedagogical trends, and attentive to systemic and structural factors that constrain effective teaching.
quotes: In Victoria, there exists a bureaucratic ratio of one bureaucrat for every two teachers, while in Queensland, this ratio stands at one bureaucrat for just under two teachers. These ratios are purportedly justified by the implementation of various educational models, school reviews, wellbeing programs, and teaching and learning incentives. However, none of these initiatives have demonstrated positive outcomes.

TPAA is part of the Red Union movement and grew to prominence during COVID by opposing vaccine mandates. In 2024, a group of education academics wrote a paper condemning TPAA as an astroturf organisation. However, if you read their paper, you will see they provide little evidence for this.

Significantly, the authors also disclose they are supporters of traditional unions, one of which funded their research into TPAA -- research that mainly involved looking at TPAA's social media accounts.

The paper rightly identifies critical pedagogy as a malign influence that the current system does not weed out due to a lack of reality checks and accountability. If it were only critical pedagogy we had to deal with, then that would be an improvement on the current situation in which we are bombarded by bad ideas from everywhere.

In his covering letter, Scott Stanford, the national president, notes that traditional unions donate to the Australian Labor Party. He does not object to this but he suggests there should be industrial representation available for people who don't want to subsidise a political party. Which is a fair point.
